title: Supporting Students’ Reading and Cognition with AI
venue: Proceedings of Workshop on Tools for Thought (CHI ’25 Workshop on Tools for Thought)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI tools shape students’ reading processes and cognitive engagement in higher education. The authors are motivated by the rapid uptake of generative AI for study support and the concern that, while AI may improve comprehension and efficiency, it may also encourage more passive reading and reduce deeper critical engagement. The study asks how students actually use AI while reading assigned course materials and how the cognitive level of their prompts changes both within a session and over time.

The study was conducted in an upper-level undergraduate AI course where students could use AI tools to assist with reading assigned materials instead of submitting a traditional written response. Students mainly used tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude. The researchers collected prompt logs, AI responses, student reflections, and discussion questions, focusing on the first three weeks of course activity. After excluding three participants whose prompts duplicated assignment-sheet text, the final analysis covered 124 reading entries from 19 students. Prompts were coded using Bloom’s Taxonomy categories to analyze levels of cognition, and qualitative reflections were examined to understand students’ perceived experiences.

The findings show that most AI prompts focused on “Understanding,” indicating that students primarily used AI for summarization and comprehension support. However, second and third prompts within a session more often involved “Analyzing” and “Evaluating,” suggesting some movement toward higher-order thinking after initial comprehension was established. Over the three-week period, though, prompts became increasingly concentrated in the “Understanding” category, which the authors interpret as a shift toward more passive engagement with reading. Students’ submitted discussion questions were more frequently analytical than their prompts, indicating that AI use may still support deeper questioning even when direct AI interactions remain surface-level.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI can help students read more efficiently, understand difficult material, and sometimes support critical thinking, but without deliberate scaffolding students may default to shallow, summary-oriented use. The authors recommend future AI reading-support systems include structured scaffolds for low-level cognitive tasks, proactive prompts for analysis and evaluation, adaptive support features, and human-in-the-loop customization by both students and instructors.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot used for conversational question answering, explanation, summarization, and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in an undergraduate course used ChatGPT to support assigned academic reading, including summarizing texts, explaining terminology, asking follow-up questions, and generating discussion questions. The paper reports that students mostly used ChatGPT among several tools.

findings.finding_summary: In analysis of 124 AI-assisted reading entries from 19 students over the first 3 weeks of a course, most prompts were coded as 'Understanding,' while 'Analyzing' and 'Evaluating' became more prevalent in second and third prompts within a session, suggesting movement toward higher-order thinking during short interaction sequences. Over time, however, Week 3 prompts were 92.86% 'Understanding' versus about 80% in Weeks 1 and 2, indicating a shift toward more passive comprehension-oriented use.
findings.measure: Bloom's taxonomy coding of reading-support prompts across prompt sequence and weeks

findings.finding_summary: Students' submitted discussion questions after AI-supported reading were predominantly higher-order, with 54.69% coded as 'Analyzing,' 34.38% as 'Understanding,' 6.52% as 'Applying,' and 4.68% as 'Evaluating.' The authors interpret this as evidence that AI-supported reading may help students formulate more analytically oriented class discussion questions.
findings.measure: Bloom's taxonomy coding of submitted discussion questions

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative reflections indicated that students perceived AI support as beneficial for reading efficiency, concise summaries, understanding difficult terminology, digestible formatting, access to external resources, and encouragement of critical thinking. These findings are based on students' self-reported experiences rather than validated outcome assessments.
findings.measure: Student qualitative reflections on AI-supported reading

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot used for conversational explanation, summarization, and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in an undergraduate course used Gemini as one of the AI tools to assist with assigned readings, including summarization and follow-up questioning.

identified_tools.name: Perplexity
identified_tools.description: A generative AI answer engine/chat assistant that supports question answering and synthesis, often with external information retrieval.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in an undergraduate course used Perplexity as one of the AI tools to support reading comprehension and questioning around assigned texts.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's generative AI chatbot used for conversational explanation, summarization, and interactive question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in an undergraduate course used Claude as one of the AI tools to support assigned reading through summaries, explanations, and follow-up prompts.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods observational study of authentic classroom use, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental design and does not report causal effect estimates. Findings are based on prompt coding and qualitative reflections from a small sample.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports suggestive positive and mixed patterns in cognitive engagement, but no standardized learning outcomes or effect sizes are reported. Impact is therefore unclear and modest at best based on available evidence.
